flashcards.a: A loop around a stateless model: send messages + tool schemas, model returns text (done) or tool calls, execute them, append results, repeat. ~40 lines.

flashcards.q: Why is agent cost quadratic in turns?
flashcards.a: The model is stateless. Every turn re-sends the entire message history, so turn N pays for turns 1..N. Total cost grows as the square of turn count.

flashcards.q: The six stop conditions for an agent loop?
flashcards.a: 1) model returns no tool call 2) step cap (10-25) 3) token budget 4) cost budget 5) wall-clock deadline 6) no-progress detector.

flashcards.q: Which stop condition fires most often in production?
flashcards.a: The no-progress detector. The common failure isn't infinite exploration, it's the model repeating an identical tool call that will never succeed.

flashcards.q: How do you implement no-progress detection?
flashcards.a: Hash (tool_name, sorted args) into a counter. At 3 repeats, return a tool RESULT telling the model to change approach - not an exception.

flashcards.q: What happens when a tool throws?
flashcards.a: Catch it and return a readable error string as the tool result, so the model can route around it. Propagating the exception discards all prior work in the run.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT catch a tool exception?
flashcards.a: When it's a bug in your harness rather than the tool's dependency. A model cannot fix your KeyError - crash loudly instead of shipping an agent that looks merely stupid.

flashcards.q: Agent reliability math at 95% per step?
flashcards.a: 0.95^10 is about 60%. At 85% per step, 10 steps is about 20%. 0.95^50 is 8%. Reliability is multiplicative.
Not a better model. Fewer steps, checkpointing so failures resume instead of restart, and human approval at consequential points.
1) Truncate tool results at the tool boundary (highest leverage) 2) Compact at ~70% of window: recap old turns, keep recent verbatim 3) Externalise to file/store so state survives compaction.

flashcards.q: What must never be compacted away?
flashcards.a: messages[0] / the system prompt, the original task statement, and any pending obligation. Carry an explicit open-items list through every compaction.

flashcards.q: What does a framework like LangGraph actually give you?
flashcards.a: Persistence and checkpointing (the real reason), streaming, interrupt()/HITL, per-node retry semantics, observability hooks, subgraph composition. NOT the loop.

flashcards.q: When is an agent the WRONG choice?
flashcards.a: When the steps are known in advance - write the pipeline. When one prompt suffices. When work is long-running or multi-party - use a durable workflow engine.

flashcards.q: Difference between ReAct and the agent loop?
flashcards.a: ReAct is the prompting pattern (interleave reasoning and action). The loop is the harness executing it. ReAct originally parsed Thought/Action/Observation text; native tool calling replaced that.

flashcards.q: How do you make a mutating tool safe to retry?
flashcards.a: Idempotency keys: client generates a key per logical operation, server stores (key to result) and returns the stored result on repeat. Read-only tools are naturally safe.

flashcards.q: How do you test a nondeterministic agent?
flashcards.a: Separate layers. Harness (stops, budgets, dispatch, compaction) is deterministic - unit test against a scripted fake model. Tools tested independently. Only end-to-end needs eval-style golden trajectories.

flashcards.q: Why does human-in-the-loop force durable execution?
flashcards.a: A human may take a day to approve. You must persist loop state before the consequential action and rehydrate on approval - an in-process loop cannot survive that wait.

flashcards.q: Single agent with 20 tools, or 5 specialists with 4 each?
flashcards.a: Start with one agent and good tools. Multi-agent costs routing errors, handoff context loss, harder debugging, more latency. Split only for parallelisable subtasks, needed context isolation, or differing permissions.
